drafts.title: $406 per pothole hit, and the flood just chewed up Colorado roads (MAIN, today ~noon)
drafts.angle: EV owner costs nobody talks about. The battery isn't what gets you, it's tires and wheels. Winter plus flood-damaged roads down south make it timely. Plus the FSD "pothole button" idea Tesla owners keep asking for.
bullets: AAA: average pothole repair bill was $406 (2022 survey); about 44 million US drivers paid one, up 57% from the year before, and they averaged two repairs.
AAA cost guide: about $200 per tire, $200 per rim, $100 front alignment ($200 four-wheel), $400 to $900 per pair of shocks or struts.
Pothole damage usually falls under collision coverage minus your deductible, so a $500 to $1,000 deductible can make a claim pointless.
Tesla owners are pushing for a "pothole / bad road" choice in FSD intervention feedback after a Scottsdale owner reportedly blew two tires on day three (X story summary, verify before citing).
drafts.body:
$406. That's AAA's average bill for one bad pothole. And most people who hit one end up paying twice in a year.

My Model Y [has eaten ___ / cost me $___ for a tire] on [road near GJ]. EVs are heavy and the low-profile tires don't forgive much.

With the flood damage down south, it's going to be a rough winter on Colorado roads. I check my tire pressure [every ___] once it gets cold, and I know my deductible is [$___], so a single tire isn't worth a claim.

Tesla folks keep asking for a "pothole" button in the FSD feedback screen so the car learns the bad spots. I'd use it every day.

Would you?
drafts.ocr_why: Dollar opener every driver feels, first-hand fill-in, easy yes/no reply.
drafts.pixel: 10 seconds kneeling by a wheel: "This is what $200 looks like. Here's the stretch of road I dodge every week."
drafts.target: Quote the biggest verified Tesla owner account posting the FSD pothole-feedback request (search "FSD pothole" on X before posting).

drafts.title: $56,250 fine, and after 71 years Disneyland's gas Autopia goes electric (tonight ~9 PM, top slot)
drafts.angle: Pure nostalgia and a smile, no sermon. A lot of us learned to "drive" on Autopia breathing lawnmower fumes. The grandkids get a quiet one.
bullets: Disneyland must retire Autopia's gas cars by Feb 1, 2027 under a California Air Resources Board settlement over uncertified Honda engines, with a $56,250 penalty (KTLA).
Disney is testing an electric prototype.
Bob Gurr, who designed the original 1955 cars, says the new version will run on a powered track instead of a battery in each car; Disney hasn't confirmed the design (Fantasyland News).
The ride opened with the park in 1955, 71 years ago.
drafts.body:
$56,250 fine, and after 71 years Disneyland's gas Autopia is going electric.

I rode it [in 19__ / with my grandkids in ___]. What I remember most is [the fumes / the bumper hitting the rail / my dad laughing ___].

Funny thing is, the first "car" a lot of us ever drove was a little gas buggy on a track. Now the next generation's first car will be electric and quiet.

[My Model Y is quieter than that thing ever was.]

Did you ride Autopia as a kid? Got a photo?
drafts.ocr_why: Human moment, huge reply bait for 45+, zero politics. Best with an old photo.
drafts.pixel: Hold up an old Disneyland photo if you have one: "That's me on Autopia in 19__. Smelled like a lawnmower."
drafts.target: Quote a big verified Disney fan account or EV account posting the KTLA story.

drafts.title: $___ a month since the GTE days. I asked AI what I'm actually paying for (Wed ~4 PM)
drafts.angle: AI as a money tool for normal people. Snap your phone bill, cover the account number, and ask your AI what every line is, what you don't use, and what a cheaper plan would run. Starlink phone news is the hook. Builds on your public "time to update Verizon" reply without repeating it.
bullets: SpaceX is in early talks with EchoStar to buy Boost Mobile or use its network for Starlink Mobile; no deal is final (Washington Post via Reuters, Axios).
AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile reportedly turned down SpaceX's network-access requests (same reports).
The AI part is your own test. Black out account numbers and PINs before sharing a bill with any AI.
drafts.body:
$[___] a month to Verizon since it was GTE Wireless. That's [___] years.

So I took a picture of my bill, covered my account number, and asked my AI one question: "What is every line on here for, and what am I paying for that I don't use?"

It found [___ / $___ in fees I never noticed]. Then I asked what a cheaper plan with the same coverage would cost. Answer: [$___].

And now Starlink is trying to buy Boost Mobile. Phones off a satellite could shake this whole thing up.

I'm shopping. What do you pay a month, and who's your carrier?
drafts.ocr_why: Dollar opener, real savings, AI shown as a tool, "what do you pay" drives replies. Only post after you've actually run it.
drafts.window: Wed ~4 PM MST (Wed 8-9 AM is held for the open $7.7B fraud post; swap them if you'd rather lead with this one).
drafts.pixel: Screen-record with the account number covered: "Here's my phone bill. Watch what happens when I ask AI what I'm paying for."
drafts.target: Quote @SawyerMerritt's post on the Boost Mobile talks.

drafts.title: $0 to get my address off people-search sites. AI did the chore (Sun ~8 PM)
drafts.angle: Not another scam warning. A "let AI do the boring chore" post. Sites like Spokeo and Whitepages list your address and phone; a browsing AI can find the listings and walk through each opt-out. Great thing for adult kids to do for Mom and Dad.
bullets: AI builder Matt Shumer shared a prompt that has a browsing AI agent find people-search listings of your address and phone and submit each site's opt-out (somethingbig.ai).
Opt-outs often need an email confirmation and should be rechecked every few months, because listings come back.
Verify how your own AI handles it before posting; use your real count.
drafts.body:
$0. That's what it cost me to get my home address off sites like Spokeo and Whitepages.

I searched my own name first. My house, my phone number, even [___] were sitting there for anybody to see.

So I had my AI find the listings and walk me through each opt-out. It found [___ sites] in about [___ minutes]. A couple needed an email confirm, that's it.

If your parents are older, do this one for them. Scammers start with exactly this info.

Have you ever looked yourself up?
drafts.ocr: Strong with your real number; OK if you haven't tried it yet
drafts.window: Sun ~8 PM MST (or Wed ~7-8 AM if the week opens up).
drafts.pixel: "I searched my own name and found my house on ___ websites. Here's how I got it off."
drafts.target: Quote Matt Shumer's (@mattshumer_) original post with your result.

drafts.title: 464 miles on one charge, and it still came up 14 miles short (Fri ~noon)
drafts.angle: Ties to your own $171.56 drive home. Range keeps getting better, but the real lesson is the one you learned crossing the country: plan the stop and stop sweating.
bullets: Chasing Cars test (via InsideEVs): BMW iX3 50 xDrive went 747 km (464 miles) on one charge from Sydney toward Byron Bay, beating its 434-mile rating, but stopped about 14 miles short of the 740 km route.
The gas X3 M50 finished with about 206 miles of estimated range left.
Bjorn Nyland's steady 56 mph test got 465 miles; at 75 mph it dropped to 337 miles.
US-household take: speed matters more than the sticker number.
drafts.body:
464 miles on one charge. And it still came up 14 miles short.

That's BMW's new iX3 in a real road test. Same car at 75 mph? About 337 miles. Speed eats range, every EV, every time.

My Model Y does about [___] miles at I-70 speeds. My whole drive home from Kentucky cost $171.56, and the stops were [___ minutes / a bathroom and a coffee].

A 10 minute stop beats sweating the last mile every time.

How far do you really drive in one shot?
drafts.ocr_why: Strong with your real highway range number and a dash screenshot.
drafts.pixel: None needed; a dash screenshot of your range is the photo.
drafts.target: Quote @InsideEVs' post of the test with your $171.56 line.
